extracted.intended_audience: SNL fans and aspiring sketch comedy writers / general readers interested in behind-the-scenes TV production
extracted.subtask_description: Describes the week-long life cycle of a Saturday Night Live sketch — from tailoring ideas to a host, through writing, table reads, rewrites, rehearsals, censorship review, and final cuts before the live show. Useful as a guide to what makes an SNL sketch viable for broadcast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor writing to the host
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers meet the Host early in the week to learn what the host can and wants to do — accents, singing, dancing — and tailor sketches accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the host's skills and interests to shape material; initial ideas are often designed to signal that you're working on appropriate scenarios. Quote: 'They tell us what the host is interested in doing and what they can do... giving us an idea of how we should tailor our writing.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitch breadth / signal you're working
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers pitch initial (often 'fake') ideas in Lorne Michaels' office to show they're generating possibilities even if those ideas may never be produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These pitches can be intentionally silly or disposable; their function is to indicate creative momentum and to give the Host a sense of potential directions (example: a deliberately absurd safety-speech gag).

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed and deadline-driven output
rubrics_metrics.description: Sketches are actually written in a marathon-long Tuesday writing session that often extends into Wednesday morning; ability to produce under tight deadlines is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect long hours and unpredictable inspiration; being able to produce workable sketches quickly is a practical selection factor: 'Writing comedy is either easy or it’s impossible... I come in usually about 12:30 p.m. and I go home at like 3 a.m.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality / 'comedy gold' mining
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers 'go mining' for original, funny ideas — the aim is to find striking, memorable premises or jokes (comedy gold) amid many attempts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persistence and imagination matter; the piece should have a clear, original comedic conceit that stands out in a large pool of submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table read laughter and exposure of weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: All sketches are read at a Wednesday table read; those that get the biggest laughs (or reveal big problems) stand out in the selection process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table read reaction is a primary early test — sketches that 'get the biggest laughs' are more likely to survive, while exposed weak spots inform rewrites. John Mulaney: table moments can be more memorable than later performances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision by Lorne Michaels and head writers
rubrics_metrics.description: After the read-through, Lorne Michaels and head writers privately choose the sketches for the week; the show operates as a competitive selection ('competition of the fittest').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that authority sits with Michaels and head writers; survival requires both quality and fit with their sense of the show. 'It's like the smoke from the pope, like the picks are in.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Creator control of production elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer who creates a piece determines set, costumes, and other production elements — the creator's vision guides execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear, specific creative direction from the writer helps preserve the intended comedic voice: 'That’s the only way you get pure comedy... it is truly a voice between the creator and the audience.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Willingness and ability to rewrite
rubrics_metrics.description: By Thursday writers participate in rewrite sessions (dividing into groups) and must be able to identify what 'doesn't work' and present changes at the table.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewriting skill and the ability to defend and revise material are crucial. Social skills matter too — 'you have to develop a thick skin' because coworkers will dissect your piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to standards/censorship concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Every sketch is read by SNL's standards executive to review problematic or 'over the top' content; sketches must address ethical/safety/standards concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate content review and be ready to tone down or reframe material flagged by standards; compliance with internal censorship considerations affects viability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performability — blocking, camera angles, and staging
rubrics_metrics.description: On Friday the cast and Host walk through sketches to block them and figure out camera angles; sketches must work visually and physically for TV.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sketch must translate from script to staged performance — clear blocking, camera coverage, and visual comedy increase chances of making the show. First blocking is 'very important' because it's the first time lines are said standing up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writer-as-note-giver to performers
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers give notes on performances to cast members and Hosts, guiding enunciation, delivery, and other aspects of execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should be able to communicate performance direction confidently, even to high-profile hosts (example: telling Sylvester Stallone to enunciate). Ability to provide effective notes contributes to successful execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-taped segment production quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Any pre-taped sketches are shot separately (on Fridays) and must meet production standards for those segments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-taped work is held to its own production timeline and quality expectations; technical execution and edit-readiness are part of selection viability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test/audience reaction in dress rehearsal
rubrics_metrics.description: The live dress rehearsal audience reaction (8–10 p.m.) strongly influences which sketches remain; audience laughter helps determine final cuts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows are adjusted based on real audience response; material that plays well in front of an audience is more likely to go live. Michael's observation seat and reactions are integral to final decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to accept cuts and adapt quickly
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers must handle having material cut and be ready to make last-minute changes up to two hours before showtime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emotional resilience and practical adaptability matter: 'things getting cut still hurt' but learning not to attach ego is part of succeeding. Final dash includes updating cue cards and last-minute director conversations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-constrained necessity — readiness vs. clock
rubrics_metrics.description: The show follows a hard clock ('we don’t go on because we’re ready, we go on because it’s 11:30 p.m.'), so sketches must reach sufficient readiness within the schedule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pragmatic readiness under time pressure matters; having workable material and contingency plans allows a sketch to be included even if not 'perfect.' Lorne builds in extra material each week to allow for unknowns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competitive culture fosters not being 'precious'
rubrics_metrics.description: The internal selection system teaches writers to move on and to not be overly attached to any single sketch, implying a cultural criterion: flexibility and team-orientation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collaboration and willingness to iterate or abandon ideas are valued traits; surviving the process requires both resilience and a team mindset.
